questions.stem: A 64 year old man is under general anaesthesia for a hip revision and is given a unit of red cells. Ten minutes later his BP falls from 128/76 to 78/42 mmHg, his temperature rises to 38.6°C and the urine in his catheter bag turns dark red. The surgeon notes new oozing from the wound edges.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fever, hypotension and haemoglobinuria minutes into a red cell unit mean ABO-incompatible acute haemolysis; oozing suggests DIC. Anaphylaxis gives hypotension without fever or haemoglobinuria.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Within minutes: fever, hypotension, haemoglobinuria and oozing (DIC). Under anaesthesia the patient cannot report back pain.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction.

elim: Gives hypotension and bronchospasm without fever, and no haemoglobinuria.
Mild fever and chills without hypotension or dark urine.
Causes hypertension and pulmonary oedema, not hypotension and haemoglobinuria.
Main feature is severe hypoxaemia; it does not cause haemoglobinuria.

steps.x: **A. Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction.** Fever + hypotension + dark urine minutes into red cells = acute haemolytic reaction.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man is transfused red cells after an upper gastrointestinal bleed. Before the transfusion his temperature was 37.2°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 106/72 mmHg. Three hours after starting he feels cold and shivery. His temperature is now 38.3°C, pulse rate 92 bpm, BP 122/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. He has no rash or wheeze.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fever and chills with normal BP, saturations and no rash is a febrile non-haemolytic reaction, caused by cytokines and usually mild. Haemolysis or sepsis would drop the BP.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Isolated fever and chills, with stable and improving observations.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction.

elim: Would cause hypotension, loin pain and haemoglobinuria, usually within minutes.
Causes hypotension and wheeze without fever.
Causes high fever with rigors, hypotension and shock.
Causes breathlessness and hypertension without fever.

steps.x: **D. Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction.** Fever alone with stable observations = febrile non-haemolytic reaction.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman with thalassaemia is having her regular red cell transfusion. After 40 minutes she notices itchy raised wheals on her forearms and neck. She has no lip swelling, wheeze or breathlessness. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 80 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An urticarial rash with normal observations and no airway or breathing features is a minor allergic reaction. Any wheeze, angioedema or hypotension would make it anaphylaxis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: no lip swelling, wheeze or breathlessness
steps.x: Urticaria only, with normal observations.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Minor allergic reaction.

elim: Gives fever, hypotension and loin pain, not isolated wheals.
Would include airway, breathing or circulation problems such as wheeze, angioedema or hypotension.
Gives fever and chills, not urticaria with normal temperature.
Occurs days to weeks later with fever, rash, jaundice and pancytopenia.

steps.x: **D. Minor allergic reaction.** Urticaria alone with normal obs = minor allergic reaction.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman is given fresh frozen plasma before a liver biopsy. Within 3 minutes she becomes hoarse with swollen lips, widespread urticaria and an audible wheeze. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 136 bpm, BP 74/40 mmHg and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Angioedema, acute wheeze, urticaria and hypotension without fever is anaphylaxis, which is life-threatening. A minor allergic reaction has normal observations.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Angioedema, wheeze, urticaria and hypotension without fever, within minutes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Anaphylactic reaction.

elim: Would cause fever and loin pain; FFP contains no red cells to haemolyse.
Urticaria alone with normal observations; she has airway and circulation compromise.
Causes hypertension and a raised JVP, not angioedema and wheeze.
Causes hypoxaemia but not angioedema and urticaria, and develops over hours.

steps.x: **B. Anaphylactic reaction.** Hypotension without fever + wheeze + angioedema = anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: An 84 year old woman with ischaemic cardiomyopathy and chronic kidney disease is given two units of red cells for a haemoglobin of 68 g/L. Near the end of the second unit she becomes breathless. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 178/96 mmHg and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. Her JVP is raised and there is a third heart sound.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: TACO is volume overload: breathlessness, hypertension, raised JVP and S3 without fever, especially with cardiac or renal impairment. TRALI gives hypotension and a normal JVP.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: ischaemic cardiomyopathy and chronic kidney disease
steps.x: Breathless, hypertensive, raised JVP and S3, no fever, with heart and kidney disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload.

elim: Causes fever and hypotension, not hypertension and a raised JVP.
Causes hypotension and angioedema, not hypertension.
Causes fever without breathlessness.
Causes hypotension with a normal JVP.

steps.x: **D. Transfusion-associated circulatory overload.** Breathless + hypertension + raised JVP after transfusion = TACO.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man with liver cirrhosis is given four units of fresh frozen plasma during variceal banding. Two hours later he is acutely breathless. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 88/54 mmHg and oxygen saturation 84% on 15 L/min oxygen. His JVP is not raised. A chest X-ray is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates with a normal heart size: non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: TRALI occurs within 6 hours, often after FFP, with severe hypoxaemia unresponsive to oxygen, hypotension and a normal JVP. TACO gives hypertension and a raised JVP.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: four units of fresh frozen plasma
steps.x: Within 6 hours of FFP: severe hypoxaemia unresponsive to oxygen, hypotension, normal JVP, bilateral infiltrates.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Transfusion-related acute lung injury.

elim: FFP has no red cells, and the main problem is hypoxaemia, not haemoglobinuria.
Gives wheeze, angioedema and urticaria within minutes.
Gives unilateral consolidation, usually in the right lower zone, and responds to oxygen.
Causes hypertension and a raised JVP.

steps.x: **E. Transfusion-related acute lung injury.** Hypoxic + hypotensive + normal JVP within 6 hours of FFP = TRALI.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man is having chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma. Three weeks after a red cell transfusion he develops fever, a widespread erythematous rash and yellow sclera. Investigations: Hb 72 g/L (130–170), WCC 0.9 x10^9/L (4–11), platelets 18 x10^9/L (150–400) and bilirubin 64 µmol/L (<21).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: TA-GvHD occurs 2 days to 6 weeks after transfusion in immunosuppressed or Hodgkin's patients, with fever, rash, jaundice and pancytopenia. Acute reactions happen within hours.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Immunosuppressed (Hodgkin's), weeks after transfusion: fever, rash, jaundice, pancytopenia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease.

elim: Occurs within minutes, not 3 weeks later, and does not cause pancytopenia.
Occurs during or soon after the transfusion and is mild.
Gives urticaria during the transfusion, not jaundice and pancytopenia.
Occurs within 6 hours with respiratory failure.

steps.x: **D. Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease.** Hodgkin's + fever, rash, jaundice, pancytopenia weeks later = TA-GvHD.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman with acute myeloid leukaemia is given a pool of platelets. Twenty minutes in she has violent rigors. Her temperature is 40.1°C, pulse rate 138 bpm, BP 76/40 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. She has no rash, wheeze or loin pain. Her blood group matches the unit.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Platelets are stored at room temperature, so they are the product most likely to be contaminated with bacteria, causing high fever, rigors and septic shock. FNHTR is mild with stable observations.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: Her blood group matches the unit
steps.x: Septic shock within minutes of a platelet transfusion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Bacterial contamination of the unit.

elim: Unlikely with a group-matched platelet unit and no loin pain.
Gives hypotension without fever, with wheeze or angioedema.
Mild fever with stable observations, not septic shock.
The main problem would be severe hypoxaemia; her saturations are normal.

steps.x: **C. Bacterial contamination of the unit.** High fever + shock after platelets = bacterial contamination.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with myelodysplasia develops rigors, a temperature of 39.8°C and hypotension 15 minutes into a platelet transfusion. The unit is returned to the laboratory. Gram stain of the bag contents shows Gram-positive rods that form spores.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Room-temperature platelet units suit skin organisms such as Staphylococcus epidermidis and Bacillus cereus; a spore-forming Gram-positive rod is Bacillus cereus.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Spore-forming Gram-positive rod in a contaminated platelet unit.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Bacillus cereus.

elim: A Gram-negative rod that does not form spores.
A Gram-negative diplococcus.
Gram-positive cocci, not spore-forming rods.
A Gram-negative rod, linked to refrigerated red cells.

steps.x: **A. Bacillus cereus.** Contaminated platelets: Staph epidermidis or Bacillus cereus.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man has a major haemorrhage after a road traffic collision and receives eight units of packed red cells over 90 minutes. His ECG is shown (see item resources). Investigations: Na 138 mmol/L (135–145), urea 7.2 mmol/L (2.5–7.8), creatinine 98 µmol/L (60–120).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the ECG change?
o: Hyperkalaemia from the transfused red cells
questions.e: Stored packed red cells leak potassium, so rapid or large-volume transfusion can cause hyperkalaemia, shown by peaked T waves. Hypokalaemia flattens T waves.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: eight units of packed red cells
steps.x: Peaked T waves after large-volume packed red cells.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hyperkalaemia from the transfused red cells.

elim: Massive transfusion causes low calcium from citrate, and high calcium does not give peaked T waves.
Causes flat T waves and U waves, not peaked T waves.
Causes J waves and bradycardia.
Causes ST elevation in a territory, not tall tented T waves across the leads.

steps.x: **B. Hyperkalaemia from the transfused red cells.** Large-volume packed red cells = hyperkalaemia risk.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman is 15 minutes into a red cell transfusion on a surgical ward. The nurse records new observations: temperature 37.9°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. She feels a little itchy on her arms.
questions.q: Which observation is the most concerning sign?
o: Respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute
questions.e: Hypotension during a transfusion is the single most concerning sign and means stop immediately, whatever the cause. Fever or itch alone are often mild reactions.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: 15 minutes into a red cell transfusion
steps.x: One observation separates a serious reaction from a mild one.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Blood pressure of 84/50 mmHg.

elim: Suggests a minor allergic reaction, usually mild.
Within normal limits.
At the upper end of normal.
A low-grade fever occurs in mild febrile reactions.

steps.x: **A. Blood pressure of 84/50 mmHg.** Hypotension during transfusion = most ominous sign: stop now.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman is having a red cell transfusion for iron deficiency anaemia from menorrhagia. Her doctor checks her history to judge her risk of an immune-mediated transfusion reaction. She has asthma, eats a vegetarian diet, runs marathons, has had four pregnancies and takes the combined oral contraceptive pill.
questions.q: Which feature of her history most increases her risk of an immune transfusion reaction?
questions.e: Previous transfusions and pregnancy expose the immune system to foreign blood cell antigens, forming antibodies that cause later reactions. The other features do not.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Exposure to foreign blood cell antigens creates antibodies.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Four previous pregnancies.

elim: Not a risk factor for alloimmunisation.
Raises VTE risk, not transfusion reaction risk.
No effect on alloimmunisation.
Explains iron deficiency, not transfusion reactions.

steps.x: **C. Four previous pregnancies.** Risk factors: previous transfusions and pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man develops acute breathlessness 2 hours into his third unit of red cells. His temperature is 37.0°C and oxygen saturation 88% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows bilateral pulmonary oedema. The team are deciding between circulatory overload and transfusion-related acute lung injury.
questions.q: Which additional finding would most support transfusion-associated circulatory overload?
questions.e: TACO is cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from volume overload, so the JVP is raised and the BP high. TRALI is non-cardiogenic: hypotension, normal JVP and refractory hypoxaemia.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: his third unit of red cells
steps.x: Both cause bilateral oedema; the JVP and BP separate them.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Raised JVP with hypertension.

elim: Fever points away from TACO, which has none.
This is the pattern of TRALI.
Typical of TRALI.
Suggests an allergic reaction or anaphylaxis.

steps.x: **D. Raised JVP with hypertension.** TACO: high BP, high JVP. TRALI: low BP, normal JVP.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman develops loin pain, fever and hypotension 15 minutes into a red cell transfusion. The transfusion is stopped and fluids are started. Her Hb has fallen and LDH and bilirubin are raised. The haematologist wants a test that shows antibody or complement coating her red cells.
questions.q: Which investigation result would confirm an immune haemolytic reaction?
questions.e: The direct antiglobulin test (Coombs) confirms immune haemolysis and is positive in a haemolytic transfusion reaction, where recipient antibody and complement coat the donor cells.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this stage.
The test detecting antibody or complement on red cells is the DAT (Coombs).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Positive direct antiglobulin test.

elim: A late marrow response that does not prove antibody-mediated destruction.
Reflects iron stores, not haemolysis.
A negative test points away from immune haemolysis.
Shows myocardial injury, not haemolysis.

steps.x: **D. Positive direct antiglobulin test.** Suspected haemolytic reaction: DAT positive confirms it.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man becomes feverish with back pain 20 minutes into a red cell transfusion. The transfusion has been stopped and his airway, breathing and circulation are stable. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. The doctor wants to know whether red cells are being destroyed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate set of investigations?
o: Chest X-ray and arterial blood gas
FBC, U&Es, LDH, bilirubin and haptoglobin
questions.e: Diagnosis is clinical combined with haemolysis testing: FBC, U&Es and a haemolysis screen (low Hb, raised LDH and bilirubin, low haptoglobin).

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this stage.

clues: back pain 20 minutes into a red cell transfusion
whether red cells are being destroyed
steps.x: A haemolysis screen: Hb, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin, plus U&Es for kidney injury.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: FBC, U&Es, LDH, bilirubin and haptoglobin.

elim: Assess lung injury, not haemolysis.
Investigate PE, not haemolysis.
Investigate anaphylaxis, not red cell destruction.
Irrelevant to an acute reaction.

steps.x: **C. FBC, U&Es, LDH, bilirubin and haptoglobin.** Suspected haemolysis: FBC, U&Es, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin (+ DAT).

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman develops rigors and a temperature of 39.6°C 25 minutes into a platelet transfusion. Her BP is 84/52 mmHg. The transfusion is stopped, IV access is maintained with saline and the bag is clamped. The doctor is deciding what to do with the unit.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in investigation?
o: Blood cultures from the patient and return the bag to the laboratory
Discard the bag in the clinical waste
Repeat the full blood count in 24 hours
questions.e: If a septic reaction is suspected, send blood cultures and return the blood bag to the laboratory to culture it and re-check compatibility. Never discard the unit.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this stage.

clues: deciding what to do with the unit
steps.x: Possible bacterial contamination: culture the patient and the unit.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Blood cultures from the patient and return the bag to the laboratory.

elim: Destroys the evidence needed to identify contamination or incompatibility.
Too slow and does not identify a septic cause.
A septic reaction must never be restarted.
Investigates anaphylaxis; she is febrile and shocked, suggesting sepsis.

steps.x: **A. Blood cultures from the patient and return the bag to the laboratory.** Septic reaction: blood cultures + send the bag back to the lab.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man is 10 minutes into his second unit of red cells after a bleed. He develops rigors and lower back pain. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 92/58 mmHg. The nurse asks whether to take blood for a haemolysis screen first.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first action?
questions.e: Stopping the transfusion immediately is the first step for any suspected reaction, before investigations. Then check the patient, send tests and return the bag.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this stage.
Any suspected reaction: the first step comes before any test.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stop the transfusion.

elim: Treats a mild febrile reaction, but this looks haemolytic.
Investigations come after stopping the transfusion.
Needed, but only after stopping the transfusion.
Any amount of incompatible blood worsens the reaction.

steps.x: **E. Stop the transfusion.** Suspected reaction: STOP the transfusion first, then investigate.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man arrives in the emergency department after a stabbing with a systolic BP of 70 mmHg. He needs red cells immediately. His blood group is not known and there is no time to wait for a group and crossmatch.
questions.q: Which red cells are most appropriate to give?
questions.e: Group O red cells lack A and B antigens, so they are compatible with everyone; O RhD negative is used when the group is unknown. AB cells are the least compatible.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this stage.

clues: His blood group is not known
steps.x: Unknown group in an emergency: the red cells compatible with everyone.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Group O RhD negative.

elim: Would cause acute haemolysis if he is group O or B.
AB cells react with anti-A or anti-B in most patients.
Would cause haemolysis if he is group O or A.
Group O, but RhD negative is preferred when the group is unknown.

steps.x: **D. Group O RhD negative.** Unknown group, emergency = O RhD negative red cells.

questions.stem: A hospital blood bank has a single spare unit of group B RhD positive red cells nearing its expiry date. Five patients on the ward need red cell transfusion. Their groups are listed as the options.
questions.q: Which patient can safely receive this unit?
questions.e: B and AB patients can receive B blood, because they have no anti-B. Groups A and O make anti-B and would haemolyse the cells.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this stage.
B cells go to patients without anti-B: groups B and AB.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Group AB RhD positive.

elim: Has anti-B, and is RhD negative.
Has anti-B, which would cause haemolysis.
Has anti-A and anti-B, and is RhD negative.
Has anti-B, which would cause haemolysis.

steps.x: **C. Group AB RhD positive.** B red cells: only B or AB recipients.

questions.stem: Before a transfusion, a bedside grouping card is tested with a patient's blood. Agglutination occurs in the anti-A well. There is no agglutination in the anti-B well or the anti-D well. The control well is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most likely blood group?
questions.e: Agglutination with anti-A only means A antigen without B or D: group A RhD negative.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this stage.

clues: Agglutination occurs in the anti-A well
no agglutination in the anti-B well or the anti-D well
steps.x: Agglutination shows the antigen is present: A present, B absent, D absent.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A RhD negative.

elim: That would also agglutinate with anti-D.
That would also agglutinate with anti-B.
That would agglutinate with anti-B, not anti-A.
That would not agglutinate with anti-A.

steps.x: **A. A RhD negative.** Anti-A agglutination only = A negative.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman with myelodysplasia is having a red cell transfusion. After 90 minutes her temperature rises from 36.9°C to 38.1°C and she feels shivery. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 134/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. She has no rash, wheeze or loin pain. The transfusion has been paused.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: A febrile non-haemolytic reaction is treated with IV or oral paracetamol; it is milder than haemolysis. Antihistamines are for urticaria.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.

clues: no rash, wheeze or loin pain
steps.x: A mild febrile non-haemolytic reaction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Paracetamol.

elim: Treats urticaria in a minor allergic reaction; she has no rash.
For anaphylaxis; she has no airway, breathing or circulation compromise.
For TACO; she is not breathless or overloaded.
Not needed for a mild febrile reaction.

steps.x: **E. Paracetamol.** FNHTR = paracetamol.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man with sickle cell disease is having an exchange transfusion. He develops an itchy raised rash over his chest. He has no lip swelling, wheeze or breathlessness. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 124/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Continue the transfusion and observe only
Halt the transfusion and give chlorphenamine
questions.e: A minor allergic reaction is managed by halting the transfusion and giving an antihistamine such as chlorphenamine. Adrenaline is for anaphylaxis.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.

clues: no lip swelling, wheeze or breathlessness
steps.x: Minor allergic reaction with normal observations.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Halt the transfusion and give chlorphenamine.

elim: The transfusion should be halted while the reaction is assessed.
For anaphylaxis, which needs airway, breathing or circulation compromise.
For volume overload.
For fever; he has no fever.

steps.x: **E. Halt the transfusion and give chlorphenamine.** Minor allergic: halt + antihistamine.

questions.stem: A 16 year old boy with IgA deficiency is transfused after a splenic injury. Within minutes he develops stridor, facial swelling and widespread urticaria. His pulse rate is 140 bpm, BP 70/38 mmHg and oxygen saturation 86% breathing air. The transfusion has been stopped and high-flow oxygen started.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Anaphylaxis is treated with IM adrenaline first, then steroids, bronchodilators and supportive care. IgA deficiency is the key risk factor.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.
Anaphylaxis in an IgA-deficient patient.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: IM adrenaline 500 micrograms (1:1000).

elim: The cardiac arrest dose; he has a pulse.
For circulatory overload, not anaphylaxis.
Too slow and does not treat airway or circulation compromise.
Treats a febrile reaction, not anaphylaxis.

steps.x: **A. IM adrenaline 500 micrograms (1:1000).** Transfusion anaphylaxis: stop + IM adrenaline.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man develops fever, back pain and hypotension 10 minutes into a red cell transfusion given to the wrong patient. The transfusion has been stopped and the line disconnected. His temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 82/48 mmHg. He passes dark urine.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Aggressive IV fluids with close monitoring of vital signs and urine output
Restart the transfusion at a slower rate
questions.e: Acute haemolytic reaction: stop the transfusion, give aggressive IV fluids, monitor vital signs and urine output closely, and consider ICU, to protect the kidneys.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.
ABO-incompatible acute haemolytic reaction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Aggressive IV fluids with close monitoring of vital signs and urine output.

elim: For anaphylaxis, which has no fever or haemoglobinuria.
Restricting fluid worsens kidney injury from haemolysis.
For a minor allergic reaction.
Incompatible blood must never be restarted.

steps.x: **A. Aggressive IV fluids with close monitoring of vital signs and urine output.** Acute haemolysis: stop, aggressive fluids, watch urine output.

questions.stem: An 88 year old woman with heart failure becomes breathless during her second unit of red cells. Her BP is 182/98 mmHg, pulse rate 102 bpm, oxygen saturation 88% breathing air and temperature 36.7°C. Her JVP is raised with bibasal crackles. The transfusion has been stopped and she is sitting up.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: TACO is treated by stopping the transfusion, oxygen and IV furosemide. IV fluids are for haemolysis and TRALI, not overload.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.

clues: JVP is raised with bibasal crackles
steps.x: TACO: fluid overload in a patient with heart failure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oxygen and IV furosemide.

elim: Would worsen fluid overload.
For anaphylaxis; she is hypertensive.
She has no fever.
Would increase the overload.

steps.x: **D. Oxygen and IV furosemide.** TACO = stop + oxygen + IV furosemide.

questions.stem: A 53 year old woman receives fresh frozen plasma before an emergency laparotomy. Ninety minutes later she is breathless with bilateral crackles. Her JVP is not raised. Her BP is 86/50 mmHg, temperature 37.8°C and oxygen saturation 82% on 15 L/min oxygen. The transfusion has been stopped.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: ICU referral for respiratory support, with IV fluids to support blood pressure
questions.e: TRALI needs aggressive oxygenation, often in ICU, with IV fluids to support BP. Furosemide (the TACO treatment) worsens hypotension.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.
TRALI: refractory hypoxaemia and hypotension with a normal JVP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: ICU referral for respiratory support, with IV fluids to support blood pressure.

elim: For anaphylaxis, which would cause angioedema and wheeze.
Lowers BP further and does not help non-cardiogenic oedema.
For minor allergic reactions.
Ignores life-threatening hypoxaemia.

steps.x: **A. ICU referral for respiratory support, with IV fluids to support blood pressure.** TRALI: oxygen/ICU + fluids, NOT furosemide.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man is 20 minutes into a red cell transfusion. He feels unwell, slightly breathless and hot. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 94/60 mmHg and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. The cause is not yet clear. The transfusion has just been stopped.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Oxygen and IV fluids while the reaction is assessed
Restart the transfusion once observations settle
